attempts.raw_response: He remained a potent cultural force even after his passing in December 2023. His music transcended political boundaries, offering both sharp social commentary and soulful melodies that resonated deeply with ordinary Zimbabweans. While the government viewed his lyrics as subversive, millions of fans celebrated him as a voice for the marginalized. The ban on "Wasakara" only amplified his popularity, turning him into an enduring symbol of artistic resistance against authoritarianism. Today, his legacy endures not just through his extensive discography, but through the vibrant spirit he injected into African music, inspiring generations to use their art to challenge power and celebrate identity with unapologetic authenticity.

pair.human_continuation: 'He was a freedom fighter' US-based Zimbabwean musician Thomas Mapfumo, with whom he started his career prior to independence in 1980, paid tribute to a "great musician". "He was a freedom fighter - that's what I can say about him," Mapfumo told the BBC's Focus on Africa radio programme. "I loved his voice and the way he used to write his music. He was such a great inspiration to those who were upcoming." Mtukudzi performed one of famous tracks Neria, about the strength of women and how they should take their place and not feel inferior to men, for the BBC in 2009: Affectionately known as "Tuku", his name is trending on Twitter as people pay tribute to him.
pair.prefix: His 2001 song Wasakara, meaning "You Are Too Old", was banned as it was seen as a reference to leader Robert Mugabe, who was ousted 16 years later aged 93. The singer and guitarist mixed several different styles to create his own distinctive Afro-jazz sound, known to his fans as "Tuku Music". In a long career he released 67 albums and toured the world.

source_document.title: Oliver Mtukudzi, Zimbabwe's Afro-jazz legend, dies
